item.title: Q1 — Tulip Parsimony and Morphological Characters
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Phylogenetic Trees & Cladistics

Kazakhstan boasts a rich ecosystem harboring numerous species of tulips, some of which are direct ancestors to many modern cultivated varieties. These tulips exhibit a diverse range of morphological traits, although not all of these traits are reliable indicators of species identification.

In Table 1 below, we outline five distinct types of tulips and their variations across five characteristics (A-E), typically utilized in the classification of tulip types.

Table 1. Morphological comparisons; A - presence/absence of hairs on the stamen, B - number of flowers (2(+) = 2 or more), C - presence/absence of a dense layer of hairs on the bulbs, D - number of leaves, E - color of the stamen filament, Y - yellow, K - black.

It’s worth noting that T. borszczowii has the same features as the common ancestor among these tulip species.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. In a phylogenetic tree constructed using maximum parsimony, the species T. lemmersii, T. salsola, and T. bifloroformis are expected to constitute a polyphyletic group.
B. The maximum parsimony tree contains at least one character reversal.
C. All plants within the genus Tulipa share the characteristic of having leaves with either arcuate or parallel veins.
D. According to the data, the presence of two or more flowers is the most recently evolved characteristic compared to the others.

item.title: Q10 — Magnetotactic Bacteria Navigation
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Cell Theory, Prokaryotes & Eukaryotes

Magnetotactic bacteria have magnetosomes (magnetite crystals with a lipid membrane) arranged in a line, helping them find water with suitable oxygen levels in the oxic-anoxic transition zone (OATZ in Figure 1B). These bacteria are classified into two types: polar, which align their body orientation with the magnetic field, and axial, which can have two orientations along the magnetic field axis. In the Earth’s Northern and Southern hemispheres, polar bacteria magnetosomes have opposite polarities. To stay in the OATZ, polar bacteria change the rotation direction of their flagella based on oxygen concentration.

Figure 1. A Magnetotactic bacteria with labeled magnetosomes, the lower image shows the magnetic field generated. B Northern hemisphere polar bacteria in water, OATZ - suitable oxygen level. C Experimental setup: water-filled tube with two openings in a magnetic field. Bacteria start in the anoxic zone (red).

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Magnetosomes help bacteria find the shortest path toward OATZ.
B. Polar bacteria from the southern hemisphere should have a clockwise flagella rotation when above OATZ.
C. Axial magnetotactic bacteria will form 2 distinct bands in experimental setup.
D. Polar magnetotactic bacteria from the southern hemisphere will start a counterclockwise rotation of flagella when placed into experimental setup.

item.title: Q11 — Directed Evolution of Enzyme D (NADH-Dependent)
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Recombinant DNA & Biotechnology Techniques

Directed evolution is a process that mimics natural selection by artificially applying selective pressure to organisms to screen and select for a desired phenotype. Directed evolution can be employed in protein engineering.

The Escherichia coli AL strain was engineered by deleting specific pathways that regenerate NAD⁺ (Figure 1). NAD⁺ regeneration can be restored by introducing a foreign enzyme, referred to as Enzyme D, which converts an exogenous substrate, not naturally connected to the native metabolic network, into a non-toxic product using NADH as a cofactor. A library comprising randomized mutants of Enzyme D is introduced into the engineered E. coli AL strain.

Figure 1. A: exogenous substrate present in large intestine; B: library variants of enzyme D; C: carbon source; D: enzyme D.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Library construction is not required for directed evolution, as Enzyme D can mutate after selective pressure is applied.
B. Enzyme D is under selective pressure only when the strain AL is growing under aerobic conditions.
C. This method of directed evolution allows for differentiating between variants of NADH-dependent enzymes with low activity or high activity, in order to select the variants with the highest activity.
D. E. coli AL strains with variants showing higher activity of Enzyme D have a better chance of survival in the human large intestine.

item.title: Q12 — DMSO₄ Poisoning Case Study
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Plasma Membrane Structure & Transport

A terminal cervical cancer patient arrived at the emergency room and received intravenous therapy and oxygen, but her condition did not improve. Medical personnel noticed a garlic-like odor, typically caused by sulfur-containing substances, emanating from her mouth, and white crystals formed in a blood sample taken from her. Subsequently, the medical staff began losing consciousness and having convulsions.

This 1994 incident at Riverside General Hospital was initially thought to be mass hysteria, later suspicion fell on DMSO₄: prior to admission, the patient had applied excessive amounts of DMSO-based ointments for analgesic purposes. While DMSO itself is non-toxic to humans, DMSO₄ is classified as a warfare agent. It rapidly undergoes the following reaction:

$$DMSO_4 + 2H_2O \rightarrow 2CH_3OH + H_2SO_4 \quad (1)$$

Figure 1. DMSO, DMSO₂, and DMSO₄ structures. DMSO₄ can be produced by successive oxidation reactions of DMSO and DMSO₂.

Compound DMSO DMSO₂ DMSO₄
Enthalpy of formation (kJ/mol) -150 -373 -687
Solubility in water (g/L) ≥150 150 28

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Out of the three involved substances, DMSO₂ most probably accounts for crystals in the collected blood.
B. DMSO can increase the rate of absorption of compounds through biological membranes.
C. The enthalpies of formation indicate that DMSO can rapidly change into DMSO₂ and then into DMSO₄ by being exposed to oxygen at room temperature.
D. Cervical cancer metastases in the ureters have likely restricted the only pathway of eliminating DMSO and its derivatives.

item.title: Q13 — Nitrogen Limitation of Legumes in Steppes
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Ecology

Legumes can fix nitrogen from the air. Anecdotal evidence showed industrial pollution with nitrogen and other macronutrients making legumes less fit for nitrogen-poor steppes and other grasslands, which make up half of Kazakhstan.

Figure 1. The graph shows the effect of increased nutrients on the legumes in steppe field plot study. They had control soil (CTL), as well as soil enriched with N (nitrogen), P (phosphorus), K⁺ (potassium), and combinations of these elements. The top row is the normalized change (NC) after 3 years of treatment, and the bottom row is the NC after 6 years of treatment. Letters represent NC in A) legume cover B) species richness C) biomass of legumes. Black dots represent a statistically significant difference from control. Whiskers stand for the Standard Error of Mean (SEM).

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Potassium coupled with nitrogen has a non-significant effect on legume cover.
B. Legume biomass has the opposite response to changes in soil nutrients after 3 years and 6 years of treatment.
C. The graphs support steppe being, in general, a nitrogen-limited ecosystem.
D. In analogous graphs for non-nitrogen fixing plants, the NC values for nitrogen-enriched soil will be positive.

item.title: Q14 — Latitudinal Diversity Gradient: Three Hypotheses
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Ecology

The latitudinal diversity gradient describes a common pattern in the species richness seen in most groups of organisms whereby there are fewer species in the temperate regions than in the tropics. Species richness is lowest at the poles and highest on the equator. The ubiquity of this pattern suggests the possibility of a single general explanation but our understanding of this pattern is incomplete. The current latitudinal zones arose approximately 45 million years ago, after a period in which the Earth was primarily tropical. The following three hypotheses (Figure 1A-C) could possibly explain this gradient:

Figure 1. A difference in carrying capacity. B difference in diversification rate. C difference in the starting point of diversification. Note that in each graph only one factor is changed.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. The higher variance in species age in the tropics compared to temperate regions is an argument supporting the hypothesis C.
B. The reappearance of the diversity gradient even after the global ecosystem catastrophe would argue against the hypothesis C.
C. Hypothesis B is supported if greater seasonal variation would increase the diversification rate.
D. The fact that most temperate taxa can be found in the tropics, but not vice versa, supports the hypothesis A.

item.title: Q15 — ENSO and Ecosystem Effects
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Ecology

Walker circulation is the model that describes how temperature differences across the Pacific Ocean can explain local pressure and precipitation: warm, moist air rises and dries out over the Western Pacific, flows east, becomes cold and dry and sinks over the Eastern Pacific, then returns west warming and moistening again.

Figure 1. Walker Circulation.

Alterations in Walker Circulation are called El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO). This oscillation has 3 phases: Neutral (normal Walker Circulation), El Niño (weak or reversed Walker Circulation), and La Niña (strong Walker Circulation). Here are some examples of the influence of ENSO on smaller ecosystems:

Figure 2. Top left: Global context of the smaller ecosystems mentioned. A, B, and C represent data from the corresponding ecosystems.

Location Ecosystem/Community Changes
A Great Salt Lake grazers (native species represented by 4 colors) and corixids (invasive freshwater predators) Ecosystem in years X, Y, and Z
B Australian red kangaroo population Size of kangaroo population (in thousands)
C Intertropical Convergence Zone - winds blowing the surface of the water cause upwelling of deep-nutrient-rich water Two consecutive years (C1 and C2); color represents productivity of algae ranging from low (blue) to high (red).

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. In neutral Walker Circulation, the Western Pacific has higher terrestrial ecosystem productivity than the Eastern Pacific.
B. Increase in the number of red kangaroos in 1988 was potentially caused by El Niño.
C. C1 shows pre-El Niño year and C2 is El Niño year.
D. Changes during year Y are probably caused by La Niña.

item.title: Q16 — Fractal Geometry and Scale-Dependent Resource Availability
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Ecology

Fractal geometry can be illustrated by Mandelbrot’s question: How long is the coast of Britain? The answer depends on the scale of measurement.

Analogously, ecosystems exhibit scale-dependent resource availability. For instance, measuring Admiralty Island’s coastline from the perspective of an eagle (using the distance between nests) yields 761 km, whereas considering barnacles (requiring 2 cm of space) results in 11,000 km.

Figure 1B shows the relationship between the coastline length of Admiralty Island and the scale at which it is measured, as defined by the equation on the graph. A similar relationship exists for the amount of resources available for a species that operates at a given scale, as well as for its biomass.

Figure 1. A Admiralty island. B Log-log graph of resolution (scale) and the length of Admiralty coastline; a, b - species; Q - resource available or biomass or coastline length, k - constant, L - scale, d - fractal dimension describing the complexity of the pattern, more complex patterns correspond to higher values of d.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. The graph for region 1 will have a steeper slope than the graph for region 2.
B. The number of individuals in an ecosystem consisting solely of species operating at scale b is larger than the number of individuals in an ecosystem consisting solely of species operating at scale a.
C. According to this theory, along with a decrease in the number of individuals at high trophic levels, all predators should have a larger body size than their prey.
D. Social behavior, such as the formation of herds, influences the scale of perspective.

item.title: Q17 — Water Scarcity Index (Rws) and Solutions
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Ecology

Water is a common renewable resource on Earth; however, after its use, water loses some of its properties, such as purity, heat content, and potential energy. While they eventually will be restored, this happens on a geological timescale. Less than 1% of total water is available for human use — renewable freshwater resources (RFWR) — and even from this small fraction of water, only 10% is enough to fulfill the needs of humanity. While theoretically, there is more than enough water, many regions still experience a water crisis — a lack of accessible RFWR or an inability to utilize available RFWR.

Figure 1. The world map with Rws values.

$$R_{ws} = \frac{W - S}{Q} \quad (1)$$

$$A_w = \frac{Q}{C} \quad (2)$$

Equations: Rws - water scarcity index, Aw - water crowding indicator, W - total annual water withdrawal by population, S - total water use from desalinated water, Q - RFWR, C - population size.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Higher human activity leads to shorter mean residence time of water molecules in reservoirs.
B. Low Rws indicates the absence of a water crisis
C. Correlation between Rws and 1/Aw is weaker in regions with poor water infrastructure.
D. Food import would be a better long-term solution for the water crisis in dry regions rather than water import.

item.title: Q18 — Animal Road Barrier Effect (Traffic Behavior Types)
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Mechanisms of Behavior

Roads are responsible for habitat fragmentation, impeding wildlife movement via the “Barrier effect,” which combines direct mortality from collisions with animal avoidance behaviour. Note that animal response to moving cars can resemble their reaction to natural danger stimuli. The research identified four types of animal behavioural responses (see Table 1) based on their perceived danger from traffic. Each animal species typically exhibits only one of these behavioral responses.

Behavior type Description
Speeders Their primary response to threats is to flee across the road.
Avoiders Avoid the road at much lower traffic volume and remain further from the road than other types.
Nonresponders Do not cease their movement at any level of traffic intensity.
Pausers Reduce their speed by freezing, which increases the time spent on the roadway.

Table 1. Types of animal behavioural responses to traffic. Traffic volume entails the number of vehicles passing a point on a road segment.

Figure 1. The total barrier effect (B, black solid line) from mortality (M, blue dashed line) and avoidance (A, red dotted line) for the four response categories. X - traffic volume in arbitrary units. Y - magnitude of the barrier effect in term probability (from 0 to 1).

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Nonresponding behaviour is more likely to exist in top predators of a food chain.
B. Relative steadiness in the mortality of mule deer after an initial increase during low traffic volume is due to the mule deer's road-avoiding behaviour.
C. Point Z indicates the moment when armadillos are more likely to start pausing at the road edge than the road surface
D. Indiana bat is probably a speeder.

item.title: Q19 — Cumulative Cultural Evolution in Rock Pigeons
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Development & Learning

Individual progress and subsequent social learning are important aspects of group living. The progressive accumulation of culture within a group over time is called Cumulative Cultural Evolution (CCE). The following study aimed to investigate the interplay between CCE and collective decision-making. Rock pigeons (Columba livia) building routes between two distant points were taken as a model system.

Figure 1. A In solo and pair controls the same birds fly all 60 times while in the experimental group, one of the birds is replaced every round (12 flights) with a new one. After each round, the performance on the last flights of the experimental pair and both controls were compared (asterisks mark a significant difference). Route efficiency is calculated relative to the straight line connecting two points. B Change in route efficiency across flights, grouped by rounds.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. There is evidence of social learning in the pigeon community.
B. Comparing the mean performance of each group within each round may lead to incorrect interpretations of the experimental results.
C. In the experimental group, the new pigeon takes an active part in developing the route.
D. Collective decision-making is the main reason for the difference between the effectiveness of the routes of the experimental group and control groups.

item.title: Q2 — Strigiformes (Owls) Phylogenetic Identification
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Phylogenetic Trees & Cladistics

You are given five species of birds from the Strigiformes order (Owls), commonly found in Kazakhstan (Figure 1A). However, the genera to which these species belong are unknown to you. To ascertain this, you were provided with information depicted in the figures below.

Figure 1. A Five bird species; the bottom row in each box represents the partial list of the birds’ inhabiting areas (refer to Figure 2). B Phylogenetic tree of the Strigiformes order with their full inhabiting area lists. The number of species that make up the corresponding genus is indicated in parentheses.

Figure 2. Area distribution key; each rectangle corresponds to a certain area.

It is also known that:

  • Species 3 and 5 share the most recent common ancestor that lived 5 million years ago.
  • Species 2 and 3 share the most recent common ancestor that lived 20 million years ago.
  • Species 5 and 4 share the most recent common ancestor that lived 40 million years ago.
  • The genus to which species 1 belongs has never been found in the Philippines.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. One of the five listed species is the only representative of its genus.
B. Constructing a phylogenetic tree using this data reveals that species 1 and 4 are the second most closely related among the five species.
C. Some of the five given species belong to the same genus.
D. A migration (in terms of species dispersal) from America to Africa and Eurasia is a more parsimonious explanation for the geographic distribution of Strix compared to a migration in the opposite direction.

item.title: Q20 — Haploid/Diploid Organisms and Multi-Allele Genetics
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Mendel's Laws & Probability in Genetics

Imagine a planet inhabited by animal-like creatures capable of both meiosis and mitosis, where the fundamental principles of genetics apply. This species is distinguished by two alternating heteromorphic generations: haploid and diploid.

The haploid (n) generation consists of intelligent beings who dwell in urban environments and form pairs of sexual partners. In contrast, individuals of the diploid (2n) generation are non-rational and aggressive and are reared in specialized nurseries. The haploid pairs entrust their offspring to these nurseries, where the diploid organisms give rise to a new haploid generation.

In one locus of these organisms, there are three alleles: A1 (most dominant) > A2 > A3 (most recessive). Among the 2n generation, 1% of organisms have the A3 phenotype, 8% have the A2 phenotype, and 91% have the A1 phenotype. The entire population is in genetic equilibrium.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Individuals with the A1 phenotype make up more than 75% of the haploid generation.
B. There are two possible genotypes for individuals with the A2 phenotype in the 2n generation
C. Each haploid organism has one "grandfather" and one "grandmother", from each of which it has exactly 50% of its genetic material.
D. When a recessive lethal mutation that blocks mitosis occurs in this gene, it can persist in the population for many generations.

item.title: Q3 — Bacterial Phylogenomics (RNA Polymerase vs Transposase)
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Molecular Systematics

Yerzhan studies the evolution of four closely related bacterial strains (A, B, C, D), focusing on RNA polymerase subunit β and transposase. He reconstructed phylogenetic trees for the two corresponding genes that code for these proteins (Figure 1X, Y) using the alignment of four sequences (representative snapshot is shown on Figure 2) and the most parsimonious solution. He rooted both phylogenies using the D strain as an outgroup. Unfortunately, he realized that he forgot to properly label the datasets. Consequently, he began comparing these phylogenetic trees to the reference phylogenetic tree reconstructed from genes of ribosomal proteins (Figure 1Z).

    X          Y          Z
   ┌─ C       ┌─ A       ┌─ A
 ┌─┤         ┌─┤         ┌─┤
 │ └─ B      │ └─ B      │ └─ B
 │           │           │
 ├──── A     ├──── C     ├──── C
 │           │           │
 └────── D   └────── D   └────── D

Figure 1. Phylogenetic trees reconstructed from RNA polymerase subunit β (X or Y), transposase (X or Y) and reference genes of ribosomal proteins (Z).

Position I Position II
A GGACT A CAGTC
B CCATT B GCGTC
C GCATA C GCACA
D CGACT D GGCCA

Figure 2. Alignments of representative regions of two genes from four bacteria strains (A-D).

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Phylogenetic tree X was reconstructed from the alignment I.
B. In the Alignment I, 4 out of 5 positions are useful for determining tree's topology.
C. Phylogenetic tree X was reconstructed from the RNA polymerase subunit β.
D. Using species D as an outgroup, there are in total two possible phylogenetic tree topologies for the four species A-D.

item.title: Q4 — Tumor Microenvironment: OCR and Extracellular pH
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Bioenergetics & Central Metabolism Overview

The extracellular pH of normal tissues is typically between 7.35 and 7.45. Meanwhile, in the tumor microenvironment, extracellular pH is mildly acidic in the range of 6.5–6.9. Figure 1B provides an overview of the average extracellular pH values observed in different tumor types compared to their respective normal cells. Cancer cells also exhibit changes in the oxygen consumption rates (OCR). This phenomenon is demonstrated in Figure 1A by comparing the OCR of normal and cancer cells from three patients.

Figure 1. A Oxygen consumption rates (OCR) in arbitrary units (AU) of normal and cancer cells. B Extracellular pH of normal tissue and corresponding tumor tissue. Asterisk indicates a significant difference.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Difference in oxygen consumption between cancerous and normal cells indicates that tumor cells exhibit decreased metabolic rate.
B. Differences in extracellular pH values can be explained by the altered ratio of glucose fermentation to oxidative phosphorylation in cancer cells compared to normal ones.
C. The tumor microenvironment is typically hyperoxic due to elevated oxygen consumption by cancer cells.
D. The cancer cells of patient 3 are more heterogeneous compared to the cancer cells of the other two patients.

item.title: Q5 — Antibody Mutagenesis and Cardiac Glycoside Binding (ELISA)
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Protein Structure, Folding & Function

Mutagenesis was performed to determine the effect of single mutations in the binding site of an antibody. The mutants were analyzed for binding to four cardiac glycoside molecules: digoxin, digitoxin, digoxigenin, and ouabain. The binding properties of mutated antibodies were tested by ELISA, a technique that relies on enzyme-linked antibodies to detect target antigens. After the antibody binds to the antigen (in our case, glycoside), the enzyme linked to the antibody catalyzes the added substrate, leading to a color change that can be measured by spectrophotometry at 405 nm. The following heatmaps represent the ELISA results based on the position of change and the amino acid to which wild-type amino acid was mutated.

Figure 1. A Binding data of antibodies mutated in the positions described in the figure to the four glycosides. The absorbance, which correlates to the binding strength of digoxigenin (P), ouabain (Q), digoxin (R), and digitoxin (S) to the mutated antibodies, was linearly scaled to that of the wild-type (labeled in red) which was assigned a value of 1.0 (labels of glycosides P, Q, R, and S should not be confused with the one-letter codes of amino acids). B Differences in the structure of digoxin (R) and its three analogs. W - sugars.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. The strongest binding in position Tyr-33 was for substitution by aromatic amino acids.
B. In all shown amino acid positions, at least one substitution improves the antibody affinity.
C. Antibody with double substitution Tyr-33-Trp and Trp-100-Arg probably could be used in cardiac glycoside detection systems.
D. Sugar moieties appear to play a role in the affinities of antibodies to cardiac glycoside molecules.

item.title: Q6 — Ramachandran Plot and Peptide Bond Geometry
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Protein Structure, Folding & Function

The bonds between the central carbon atom and attached groups in peptides can rotate freely. The rotation angles of the N-Cα and Cα-C bonds are called φ (phi) and ψ (psi) angles, respectively. To measure the φ angle, first draw the Cα-C bond horizontally so that the N group is at 0 degrees (in the same plane as the Cα-C bond). Then rotate the distal N group around the Cα-C bond until the structure matches the structure that you aim to measure as shown in Figure 1C. For the ψ angle, place the N-Cα bond horizontally and rotate the distal C group. The Ramachandran plot visually represents the combinations of φ and ψ angles in a peptide backbone (Figure 1B).

Figure 1. A Part of the peptide with shown φ and ψ angles. B The Ramachandran plot with the values of φ and ψ angles for all the amino acid residues except Gly in the rabbit’s pyruvate kinase. C The φ angle values are created by the rotation. D Three structures of amino acids’ residues.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. The structure (a) in Figure 1D is located in Region 2 in Figure 1B.
B. The structure (b) in Figure 1D is located in Region 3 in Figure 1B.
C. The structure (c) in Figure 1D is uncommon in rabbit's pyruvate kinase.
D. Amino acids, other than glycine, with 0 degrees of both φ and ψ angles do not occur in rabbit's pyruvate kinase.

item.title: Q7 — Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP)
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Bioenergetics & Central Metabolism Overview

The Pentose Phosphate Pathway (PPP) is a metabolic pathway occurring in the cytoplasm that mainly generates NADPH and ribose 5-phosphate. NADPH is used for the reduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as hydrogen peroxide. PPP has oxidative and non-oxidative phases, which are irreversible and reversible, respectively.

Figure 1. A Oxidative. B Non-oxidative. G6P – glucose 6-phosphate, GA3P – glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, F6P – fructose 6-phosphate, R5P – ribose 5-phosphate, G6PDH – glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase, TKT – transketolase, N - nucleotides. CXP - other intermediates where X is the position of phosphorylated carbon. Note that all intermediates of PPP are phosphorylated on the last carbon.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. In actively dividing cells, the reactions occurring before the first TKT-catalyzed reaction are more active than those occurring later.
B. TKT catalyzes a reaction that transfers a one-carbon fragment.
C. Deficiency of G6PDH activity will reduce the level of available NADPH in red blood cells.
D. For each molecule of G6P, there will be two molecules of F6P produced through both phases.

item.title: Q8 — IGF2-H19 Imprinting and CTCF Loops
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Gene Regulation: Eukaryotic & Epigenetics

Certain loci in the genome are influenced by epigenetic modifications, but understanding their precise mechanisms remains challenging. The IGF2-H19 locus serves as a well-known example, regulated by the methylation state of the imprinting control region (ICR). In addition to the two genes, this locus contains one enhancer and four CTCF-binding sites (CTCF is a DNA-binding protein), one of which serves as an ICR. A proposed model suggests that the spatial interaction among these elements underlies the regulatory mechanism governing the expression of IGF2 and H19. CTCF binding does not interrupt with the promoter function.

Figure 1. A Paternal chromosome, IGF2 active (green arrow) and H19 inactive (red arrow). B Maternal chromosome, IGF2 and H19 basal expression (black arrows). Note that diagrams A and B reflect real physical distances and that intersection of two blue lines (representing DNA) reflects very close physical proximity of two DNA strands. C DNA loop formed by CTCF and cohesin. D IGF2-H19 locus with CTCF-binding sites 1-4 (CTCF-BS).

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. One CTCF-binding site can be involved in the formation of only one DNA loop.
B. ICR overlaps with CTCF binding site 2.
C. The enhancer is located between CTCF binding sites 3 and 4.
D. ICR methylation directly affects the expression of H19, independent of the enhancer.

item.title: Q9 — ATAD1 Mitochondrial ATPase (Cryo-EM Study)
item.description:
Theoretical A Real exam question — full text reproduced under IBO's CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license
Protein Structure, Folding & Function

Cryo-EM is a modern structural study technique that works by averaging multiple low-quality electron micrographs; cryo-EM generates high-quality structural maps. It offers flexibility by accommodating various molecular sizes and capturing multiple conformations. The structure and mechanism of ATAD1, a mitochondrial homohexamer protein, were resolved using cryo-EM. The protein’s function was then determined using the structural data and fluorescent assays.

Figure 1. A Density map of the average of all conformations obtained by electron microscopy. B Top view of the molecular model of ATAD1 hexamer emphasizing C-terminal alpha-helices, with a black curve representing the polypeptide chain substrate. C The structure of the central pore with its substrate (black) and all interacting amino acids (colored residues). D Fluorescent microscopy assay for wild-type ATAD1 and with mutation E193Q (at position 193, Glu → Gln), Gos28 is the hypothetical target, MitoTracker is a mitochondrial fluorescent marker, the red arrow points to one mitochondrion.

On your answer sheet, indicate “T” for true statements and “F” for false ones.

A. Given that the density map contains an unclear M6 subunit, at any moment only one of the ATAD1 subunits is flexible.
B. C-terminal alpha helices shown on the molecular model are made entirely from hydrophobic amino acids.
C. Change of charge due to mutation E193Q affects the physical interaction of position 193 with the substrate.
D. ATAD1 translocates proteins mislocalized into the matrix of the mitochondria.
